title: Campaign: validation at the boundaries across the estate
_note: rv2 S2 (PLAN §2.2 campaign-<tag> row, tag validation-at-boundaries). Sources are 3 live campaign study quests from different repos per idea; recapAfter = any 3 sources passed. Server-local side file, never stamped.

ideas.idea: Data from outside (request bodies, imports, storage) enters as unknown and is parsed by a schema at the boundary; a type cast is not validation.
ideas.why: Casting req.body to a type tells the compiler a story the runtime never checks, so bad input fails deep inside the code.
ideas.prompt: An import feature reads a JSON backup with `const data = JSON.parse(text) as ExportData`. A corrupted file wipes part of the user's data. What should the import look like?
ideas.answer: Parse into unknown and validate the whole payload against a schema (or an asserts function) before using any of it; refuse the file, saying what is wrong, at the first mismatch. Only after the payload is proven valid does the import touch storage, so a bad file changes nothing.

ideas.idea: Validate the complete input first, then apply it in one atomic write, so a failure leaves the old state intact.
ideas.why: Writing item by item while validating leaves half-applied imports and updates when one item turns out to be invalid.
ideas.prompt: An update endpoint changes fields one by one and throws when it reaches an invalid one, leaving the earlier changes saved. How do you restructure it?
ideas.answer: Build the complete replacement first and validate it (for example safeParse of the whole object), and only when it passes perform a single update or a single storage write. An invalid field then rejects the whole request and nothing is changed.

ideas.idea: Define each request's rules once, in the schema the boundary uses, and derive types and partial update schemas from it; duplicated rules drift.
ideas.why: Rules copied into controller, service and form disagree after the first change, so some paths accept what others reject.
ideas.prompt: A codebase defines updateTaskSchema as createTaskSchema.partial(), yet the PUT route calls createTaskSchema.parse and there is no PATCH route. What does that tell you, and what should change?
ideas.answer: The partial schema exists but is unused, so partial updates are impossible and the intent is unclear. Decide the update semantics, wire each route to the schema that matches it (PUT full, PATCH partial), and derive the TypeScript types from those schemas so code and validation cannot diverge.

ideas.idea: A validation failure answers 400 or 422 naming the field and the rule; it never echoes internal error messages that reveal what exists.
ideas.why: Returning raw exception text leaks internals and can become an oracle, while a vague 'bad request' leaves the client unable to fix anything.
ideas.prompt: An API's error handler returns error.message with status 400 for any Error. A reviewer calls it an existence oracle. Explain the risk and what the handler should do.
ideas.answer: Internal messages such as 'project 42 not found in workspace 7' tell an attacker which ids exist and how the code works. Return a structured validation body for real input errors (field, rule, message written for clients), map other known errors to their own statuses with generic text, and log the details server side.

ideas.idea: A route handler runs its checks in a fixed order (session, permission, input validation) before any domain work, so failures are cheap and consistent.
ideas.why: Validating after loading data or calling services wastes work and gives different errors for the same mistake on different routes.
ideas.prompt: Some routes return 500 for a missing session, others 401; some validate the body after querying the database. How would a shared route wrapper fix this?
ideas.answer: Put the order in one wrapper used by every route: resolve the session (401 if missing), assert the declared permission (403), parse and validate the input (400 with field errors), then call the handler and map known domain errors. Every route then fails the same way for the same reason.
